overall_summary: Space anomalies, particularly extreme planetary conditions and sensory-focused cosmic facts, are driving the highest engagement and view counts (e.g., 'Burning Ice' at 1,053 views). Conversely, abstract psychology and brain-related facts are underperforming, struggling to capture immediate swipe-by attention, and suffering from low view velocity.

winning_patterns.pattern: Extreme Planetary Conditions & Sensory Space Facts
winning_patterns.evidence: 'The Planet of Burning Ice' reached 1,053 views, 'Largest Ocean in Space' hit 460 views, and 'What Does Outer Space Actually Smell Like?' reached 368 views.
winning_patterns.action: Double down on extreme space anomalies, using physical, sensory, or highly visual descriptions (burning ice, molten iron, smells, oceans) in the titles and hooks.

weak_patterns.evidence: Videos like 'Your Brain Can Create Fake Memories' (5 views) and 'The Real Reason Songs Get Stuck In Your Head' (17 views) consistently fail to gain traction.
weak_patterns.action: Pivot away from generic brain/psychology facts unless they can be framed with a high-stakes, highly visual, or shocking historical hook.

next_video.concept: WASP-12b, the egg-shaped planet being actively consumed and stretched by its parent star.
next_video.opening_direction: Show a distorted, egg-shaped planet with the hook: 'This planet is actively being eaten alive right now.'
next_video.twist_direction: Reveal that the star's extreme gravity has stretched the planet into a football shape, and it is losing 189 quadrillion tons of mass every single year.
next_video.reason: Leverages the proven high-performance space anomaly trend, uses a highly visual physical distortion hook, and maintains a tight 15-second duration to maximize completion rate.

experiment: Test a 'Cosmic Comparison' format (e.g., comparing a bizarre space scale to an everyday object) to see if grounding abstract cosmic sizes increases retention among casual viewers.
